findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Specify `build_usage_limits` return shape explicitly as `-> tuple[UsageLimits, int, int]` (i.e. `(usage_limits, req_limit, eff_max_iter)`) so the caller's unpacking contract is unambiguous and consistent with the plan's stated invariant that `req_limit` is read from the local, not from the UsageLimits object.
evidence: Plan signature: `build_usage_limits(cfg, req, UsageLimits) -> tuple` — no tuple contents stated
runner.py:476: `req_limit = max(1, math.ceil(eff_max_iter / 2))` — a local used at line 543 (FailureContext) and line 573 (telemetry log)
runner.py:468: `eff_max_iter = effective_max_iterations(...)` — also used at line 543 and line 573

Plan 'Honest accounting' section: 'Bound to a LOCAL so the telemetry logs report it directly instead of reading it back off the UsageLimits object' — this invariant requires the tuple to carry req_limit and eff_max_iter back to the caller
ABSENCE: no AC verifies the return shape of build_usage_limits or that req_limit/eff_max_iter are unpacked correctly by the caller
findings.finding: The `build_usage_limits` return type is specified as `-> tuple` but the tuple contents are never named. The caller in `run()` needs `req_limit` and `eff_max_iter` independently AFTER the call — `req_limit` is used in `FailureContext` (not readable back from `UsageLimits`) and in the telemetry log; `eff_max_iter` is used in `FailureContext` and the log. The plan even states 'Bound to a LOCAL so the telemetry logs report it directly instead of reading it back off the UsageLimits object', which requires the tuple to carry them. An implementer following `-> tuple` literally could return just `(usage_limits,)` or only `usage_limits`, then re-derive the locals from `UsageLimits` attributes, breaking the stated invariant — or produce a function whose return shape is undiscoverable from the plan.
scenarios: Implementer returns `usage_limits` alone; caller re-derives req_limit from UsageLimits.request_limit, silently violating the plan's own stated invariant about not reading it back from the object.
Implementer returns `(usage_limits, req_limit)` but forgets `eff_max_iter`; FailureContext gets a wrong/re-derived eff_max_iter and the telemetry log is incorrect.
findings.suggested_fix: Replace `build_usage_limits(cfg, req, UsageLimits) -> tuple` with `build_usage_limits(cfg, req, UsageLimits) -> tuple[UsageLimits, int, int]` and add one sentence: 'Returns `(usage_limits, req_limit, eff_max_iter)` — all three are used independently by the caller: `usage_limits` is passed to the agent, `req_limit` and `eff_max_iter` are passed to `FailureContext` and the telemetry log (not read back from the `UsageLimits` object).'

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Add a grep proving command for the monkeypatch-repoint naming claim, e.g.: `git log -1 --format=%B <sha> | grep -E 'repoint(ed)?|monkeypatch'`, or explicitly state 'if zero repoints needed, state "no monkeypatch repoints required (measured)" in the message' and provide a grep to confirm that sentinel.

Contrast: the LOC AC has `git log -1 --format=%B <sha> | grep -E 'runner\.py (before|after): [0-9]+'`
No equivalent grep for repoint names is provided
findings.finding: The monkeypatch-repoint AC requires that any moved monkeypatch target be 'named in the message', but provides no grep proving command to verify this naming claim in the commit artifact — unlike the LOC measurement AC, which supplies a full `git log … | grep -E` command.
findings.location: Acceptance Criteria — last bullet ('any monkeypatch target that moved is repointed IN THE SAME COMMIT and named in the message')
scenarios: A reviewer cannot programmatically verify from the commit artifact that the message names the repointed targets; they must read the full commit message and cross-reference with changed test files manually.
If zero repoints were needed, a reviewer cannot distinguish 'no repoints needed (measured)' from 'repoints were silently omitted'.
findings.suggested_fix: Add to the AC: `(prove with: git log -1 --format=%B <sha> | grep -iE 'repoint|no monkeypatch')`. If zero repoints were needed, require the message to contain the literal string 'no monkeypatch repoints required (measured)' so the grep anchors to a known sentinel.

evidence: runner.py lines 47-58 re-imports everything from structured_run as module globals: `from rebar.llm.structured_run import (_extract_usage, _import_pydantic_ai, ..., effective_max_iterations, effective_max_tokens, ...)`
tests/interfaces/store/test_execution_mode_dispatch.py:87: `monkeypatch.setattr(runner_mod, '_pai_structured', _fake_structured)` — relies on `_pai_structured` being a runner module global
tests/unit/test_pydantic_ai_runner.py:382: `monkeypatch.setattr(runner_mod, '_pai_structured', _fake_structured)` — same pattern
Plan 'Monkeypatch repoints' section does not tell the implementer to add the two new functions to runner.py's top-level re-import block from structured_run
findings.finding: The plan does not enumerate the three test files that import `effective_max_iterations` and/or `effective_max_tokens` directly from `rebar.llm.runner` (`tests/unit/test_llm_failure_matrix.py:71`, `tests/unit/test_agentic_budget_and_truncation.py:24`, `tests/unit/workflow/test_plan_review_verify_recovery.py:22`). While these symbols are not being moved by this ticket, the plan instructs the implementer to add `build_model_settings` and `build_usage_limits` to runner.py's re-import list from structured_run — but does not state this explicitly, leaving open whether `run()` will call them as module globals (re-exported into runner's namespace, consistent with the established pattern) or via an inline import. If an implementer chooses the inline-import path, any future monkeypatch targeting `runner_mod.build_model_settings` would silently have no effect.
findings.location: Scope section / 'Monkeypatch repoints' section / runner.py lines 47-58 (re-import block)
scenarios: Implementer calls `build_model_settings` via an inline import inside `run()` rather than via a module global re-exported from structured_run; a future test that monkeypatches `runner_mod.build_model_settings` silently patches a dead binding and has no effect on the actual call.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a sentence to the 'Monkeypatch repoints' section: 'Add `build_model_settings` and `build_usage_limits` to runner.py's `from rebar.llm.structured_run import (...)` block at lines 47–58, following the same pattern used for `_pai_structured` and `effective_max_iterations`. findings.finding: Terminology drift between Scope and AC2/AC3: Scope calls the per-request token ceiling 'per-run request ceiling' and the iteration budget 'max_iterations', while AC2 calls it 'per-request output cap' and AC3 calls it 'per-request step budget'. An implementer cross-checking ACs against the Scope description must infer these are the same concepts.
findings.location: Scope section ('max_tokens … max_iterations … per-run request ceiling') vs AC2 ('per-request output cap') and AC3 ('per-request step budget')
scenarios: An implementer reading the Scope may implement max_iterations logic and not realize AC3 is verifying that same logic, or may implement a separate 'step budget' concept thinking it differs from max_iterations.
findings.suggested_fix: In AC2 write: 'a test asserts a per-request max_tokens ceiling can only RAISE the configured floor, never lower it'; in AC3 write: 'a test asserts a per-request max_iterations (step) budget likewise only raises'. Optionally annotate the Scope line: 'max_iterations (per-request step budget)'.
